result:
On the day the city ran out of street names, they began naming roads after things people had meant to say.

The first was I Should Have Called, a narrow lane behind the hospital. Then came You Were Right Avenue, which caused some trouble because everyone insisted it ought to be a one-way street.

By autumn, the maps were almost unbearable.

A delivery driver might spend his morning looking for a house on I Didn’t Know You Were Lonely, then turn onto Of Course You Can Come Home. Taxi passengers cried without warning. GPS voices, perfectly calm, announced: “In two hundred feet, turn left onto I Was Afraid.”

The city council received complaints.

“These are not practical names,” said a man who lived at the corner of It Wasn’t Your Fault and Please Stay.

But businesses adapted. A bakery on I Saved You Some became unexpectedly successful. Marriage proposals happened so frequently on Let’s Try Again that the pavement needed replacing.

Only one street remained unnamed.

It was a short, unremarkable road beside the reservoir. No shops. No houses. Just a bench, a railing, and water that held the evening light a little longer than seemed possible.

The council invited suggestions. Thousands arrived.

A clerk named Mara read them all. Then she submitted a blank sheet of paper.

At the meeting, someone asked whether she was making a joke.

“No,” she said. “I think we should leave somewhere for people who aren’t ready.”

The motion passed by one vote.

Years later, when strangers asked how to find the road by the reservoir, people still gave directions the old way.

Past the pharmacy. Right at the hill. Keep going until you see the water.

You’ll know it when you get there.
